author: Dennis Kelly
year_written: 2007 (commissioned for NT Connections); first performed 16 February 2008, Cottesloe Theatre, National Theatre, London
auditor_note: Factual errors only. Interpretation not flagged. Sources: LitCharts full summary and scene summaries, GradeSaver summary and character list, RevisionWorld (structure, characters, summary), StageAgent, LitCharts character pages (Adam, Leah, Phil), multiple GCSE revision guides. 15 lessons across AQA (7) and OCR (8).

fact_base.structure: Four acts; each act cycles through three locations: A Street (Mark and Jan), A Field (Leah and Phil), A Wood (whole group). Acts 1-3 each have four scenes (Street → Field → Wood → Field); Act 4 has two scenes only (Street → Field with Richard replacing Leah). Total: 14 scenes across Acts 1-4 per the Revisionworld structure guide (some sources cite 16 by counting Acts 1-3 as 4 scenes each × 3 = 12 plus Act 4's 2 = 14). Note: the user prompt states '12 short scenes alternating between three locations' — the scholarly consensus is closer to 14 or 16 depending on whether Act 4 is counted as 2 or 4 scenes. The play does NOT have exactly 12 scenes.
fact_base.premiere: 16 February 2008, Cottesloe Theatre, National Theatre, London, as part of the NT Connections programme for young performers
fact_base.adam_bullying: In Act 1 (reported by Mark and Jan): group made Adam eat leaves, light his own SOCKS on fire (not his shirt), steal vodka, accept being punched, have cigarettes stubbed out on him, and walk across a metal grille over an abandoned mine shaft while drunk — stones were thrown at him, one hit his head and he fell.
fact_base.adam_survival: Adam survives the fall — lands on a pile of leaves, crawls through a tunnel, emerges in the woods/forest, loses memory, lives in a hedge surviving on dead animals and raw rabbit. Found in Act 3 by Cathy and Brian.
fact_base.adams_death: In Act 3, Phil demonstrates how to use a plastic bag to suffocate, then sends Cathy and a heavily medicated/dissociated Brian into the woods to kill Adam (off-stage). Cathy oversees the killing. Brian is manipulated; the killing is confirmed as completed by Act 4.
fact_base.cover_up_plan: Phil's plan: steal a piece of Adam's clothing (jumper), get a random person to handle it so their DNA is on it; have Brian make a false report to the headmaster about a 'fat postman flashing genitals in the woods' to create a suspect description. Cathy takes initiative and goes to a sorting office to find a fat postman matching the fabricated description, tricks him into handling Adam's jumper. Police arrest the innocent postman. Brian is coerced into identifying him at the police station. A 'man living rough' is NOT a component of the original cover-up plan — that description conflates the plan with Adam himself (found living in a hedge in Act 3).
fact_base.postman_fate: Arrested and presumably imprisoned based on the false identification. The play does not show him being cleared — Kelly leaves this deliberately unresolved. The audience never learns if he is released.

character_fates_act4.Phil: Withdraws to the field alone, no longer eating, says nothing when Richard visits. Emotionally shut down.
character_fates_act4.Leah: Disappears — leaves without explanation; switches schools. Not present in Act 4.
character_fates_act4.Cathy: Becomes the group's new violent leader at school; Richard reports she is rumoured to have cut off a first-year student's finger. She is NOT described as going into a TV career — the 'television' element is her earlier excitement at being interviewed about Adam's disappearance (Act 2) and her fame from that clip being shown on TV. Her Act 4 fate is violent school dominance.
character_fates_act4.John_Tate: Has 'found God' — becomes an evangelist. Left the group before Act 4.
character_fates_act4.Danny: On work experience at a dentist's but hates it because the open mouths remind him of holes. His aspiration to be a dentist is psychologically damaged.
character_fates_act4.Brian: Heavily medicated, has had a breakdown, barely functioning.
character_fates_act4.Richard: Replaces Leah in the field scenes; visits Phil in Act 4, talks to him — Phil says nothing.
character_fates_act4.Lou: Has become Cathy's best friend; passive follower of the new power.
character_fates_act4.Mark_and_Jan: Continue as narrators reporting events; still the Greek chorus in Act 4 Street scene.

fact_base.cathy_cigarette: Cigarettes were stubbed out on Adam as part of the initial bullying in Act 1 (reported through Mark and Jan's fragmented retelling). There is no distinct Act 3 cigarette-torture scene. In Act 3, Cathy's violence is the killing of Adam (plastic bag, off-stage). The cigarette detail belongs to the Act 1 crime narrative, not Act 3.
fact_base.phil_food: Phil eats throughout the field scenes as a symbol of detachment. Sources confirm: ice cream (Act 1 field), muffin (Act 1 wood or Act 1 opening), chips/toffo in later acts, waffle at some point. By Act 4 he eats nothing — Kelly's signal that Leah's absence has broken him. Exact sequence per act is not definitively established from study sources; the pattern is the snacks disappearing by Act 4, not the specific order.
fact_base.milgram: Stanley Milgram obedience experiment, 1963, Yale University. 65% of participants administered what they believed were lethal 450-volt shocks when told to by an authority figure. The figure 65% is correct.
fact_base.stanford_prison: Philip Zimbardo, Stanford Prison Experiment, 1971. Voluntees assigned as guards became sadistic; experiment halted early. Correctly attributed to Zimbardo.
fact_base.bonobo_quote: Leah's key quote about bonobos: 'We share 99.6% of our DNA with them. Chimps. Not bonobos. We share more of our DNA with bonobos. But we choose chimps.' Multiple sources confirm this is the correct wording (or close to it). The figure 99.6% is used in the play.
fact_base.john_tate_quote: John Tate bans the word 'dead': 'I'm in charge and no one, I'm telling you, no one is going to use that word.' Confirmed from multiple sources.
fact_base.structure_act4_detail: Act 4 deviates from the earlier pattern: it has only 2 scenes (Street with Mark and Jan; Field with Phil and Richard). There is no Wood scene in Act 4 — the group gathering has dissolved.

findings.location: Section: What Happened to Adam — bullying list
findings.claim: "The bullying of Adam escalated from stealing vodka to setting his shirt on fire, putting a plastic bag over his head, and finally daring him to walk across a grille."
findings.issue: Adam was made to light his own SOCKS on fire, not his shirt. The item burned is socks, confirmed by LitCharts Act 1 Scene 1 summary, GradeSaver summary, and multiple GCSE revision guides. Additionally, the 'plastic bag over his head' is not part of the initial bullying narrative reported in Act 1 — the plastic bag technique appears in Act 3 when Phil demonstrates it as the method for killing Adam. In Act 1, the reported torture involves eating leaves, socks on fire, stealing vodka, being punched, cigarettes stubbed on his skin, being made drunk, walking on the grille, and stones being thrown. 'Plastic bag over his head' before the grille scene conflates Act 1 and Act 3.
findings.correction: Adam was made to light his own socks on fire (not his shirt). The sequence in Act 1 is: eat leaves, burn his socks, steal vodka, accept punching, cigarettes stubbed out on him, walk drunk across a grille — a stone was thrown and hit his head, causing him to fall. The plastic bag does not appear in Act 1's bullying; it is Phil's Act 3 killing method.
findings.source: LitCharts Act 1 Scene 1 summary ('convinced him to eat leaves, light his own socks on fire, steal alcohol, and accept being punched repeatedly'); GradeSaver summary; StageAgent summary; multiple GCSE study guides.

findings.claim: "Cathy emerges as the play's most overtly violent character in Act 3. When Adam is found, she is the one who takes charge of controlling him. She tortures Adam with a lit cigarette, burning him to establish dominance and ensure his silence. This is the play's most physically violent moment — and significantly, it is one of the few acts of violence that occurs onstage (or very close to it, depending on staging), breaking Kelly's earlier pattern of keeping brutality offstage."
findings.issue: There is no distinct cigarette-torture scene in Act 3. Cigarettes being stubbed out on Adam are part of the original bullying in Act 1, reported through Mark and Jan's fragmented street-scene narration. In Act 3, Cathy's role is to oversee Brian killing Adam with a plastic bag (off-stage) — which Kelly keeps offstage, consistent with his overall dramatic method. Multiple authoritative sources (GradeSaver, RevisionWorld, LitCharts, StageAgent) describe the Act 3 violence as Phil demonstrating the plastic bag technique to Brian and then sending Cathy and Brian off to kill Adam; none describe a cigarette scene in Act 3. Teaching students that a cigarette torture scene occurs in Act 3, onstage, is factually incorrect and would mislead exam analysis (students writing about 'the Act 3 cigarette scene' that doesn't exist).
findings.correction: The cigarette torture is part of the Act 1 crime, reported in Mark and Jan's retelling of how Adam was bullied. In Act 3, Phil demonstrates the plastic bag suffocation method to Brian and sends Cathy and Brian off to kill Adam — this killing occurs offstage, consistent with Kelly's method of keeping violence invisible. Remove the cigarette scene from Act 3. The correct description of Cathy's Act 3 violence is overseeing Adam's suffocation.
findings.source: LitCharts full summary; GradeSaver Act 3 summary (pages 49-61); RevisionWorld characters page; StageAgent summary; LitCharts Adam character page — all confirm the cigarette detail belongs to Act 1 bullying narrative, not Act 3.

findings.location: Section: Phil's Plan — Key Fact box
findings.claim: "Phil's cover-up plan has three components: (1) take Adam's DNA from clothing, (2) plant it on a fictional suspect by smearing it on a postman, and (3) use a man living rough as a fake witness."
findings.issue: The third component is wrong. Phil's plan does not involve 'a man living rough' as a fake witness. The plan involves Brian making a false report to the headmaster about a 'fat postman flashing genitals in the woods' (creating a fictional suspect description); Cathy then takes unilateral initiative to find a real fat postman at a sorting office and tricks him into handling Adam's jumper, framing him with DNA evidence. There is no separate 'man living rough' in the plan. The phrase 'man living rough' conflates Phil's cover-up plan with Adam himself — who is found in Act 3 living in a hedge in a rough state. A student memorising this three-component list would write incorrect detail in an exam.
findings.correction: Phil's plan has two core components: (1) steal Adam's jumper without touching it (using gloves), so his DNA is on the clothing; (2) have Brian make a false report to the school headmaster describing a 'fat postman' flashing in the woods, then get the jumper's DNA onto a real man matching that description (Cathy achieves this independently at the sorting office). Brian is coerced into identifying the postman at the police station. Remove 'man living rough as fake witness' from the list.
findings.source: StageAgent summary (Phil's plan described in detail); LitCharts summary; GradeSaver summary; confirmed by multiple sources that the 'man living rough' is Adam himself (found in Act 3), not a planned witness.

findings.location: Section: Cathy's Violence — Act 3 paragraph; Act 4 section
findings.claim: "By Act 4, she has joined a media career, cheerfully discussing the events as though they were an interesting story rather than a moral catastrophe."
findings.issue: Cathy does not 'join a media career' by Act 4. In Act 4, Richard reports that Cathy has become the group's new violent leader at school, and there is a rumour she has cut off a first-year student's finger. The 'television' element is Cathy's earlier excitement in Act 2 at being interviewed on TV about Adam's disappearance — Richard later reports in Act 4 that 'Cathy was on the telly' (the old news clip was re-broadcast). This is about a past TV appearance connected to the cover-up, not a new media career. Describing Cathy as having 'moved into television' or 'joined a media career' by Act 4 misrepresents her actual fate (violent school dominance, rumoured sadistic acts) and removes the play's bleakest irony — that she thrives through violence, not fame.
findings.correction: By Act 4, Cathy has become the group's dominant, sadistic leader at school. Richard reports she is rumoured to have cut off a first-year's finger. Her 'television' moment was being interviewed during the cover-up period (Act 2 period) — a news clip, not a career. Her Act 4 fate is violent power, not media celebrity.
findings.source: GradeSaver character list (Cathy 'becomes a formidable bully at school; it is rumored that she cut off a younger student's finger'); RevisionWorld characters page; LitCharts character analysis; StageAgent summary.

findings.claim: "Her success at the end is Kelly's most bitter observation: society rewards confidence and assertiveness, even when those qualities are rooted in a complete absence of moral feeling." (The earlier section in this lesson also implies Cathy is 'going into television'.) — On checking the text of this lesson, it says 'by Act 4, she is going into television.'
findings.issue: Repeats the same error as DNA-004. Cathy's Act 4 outcome is violent school dominance and rumoured sadistic violence (cutting off a finger), not a television career. The lesson's thematic argument (about society rewarding confidence) is valid as interpretation, but the factual anchor — that she goes into television — is wrong and would mislead students citing her career as evidence of Kelly's social commentary.
findings.correction: Cathy's Act 4 fate is becoming the group's most dangerous leader at school, not entering television. The bitter irony Kelly creates is that Cathy's sadism goes unpunished and she thrives within the school social hierarchy — not that she gets a media job.
findings.source: GradeSaver; RevisionWorld; StageAgent — all confirm Cathy's Act 4 fate is violent school dominance.

findings.location: Section: The Structure of the Play
findings.claim: "DNA has four acts, each preceded by a short scene between Mark and Jan on a street. These 'street' scenes function like a Greek chorus, drip-feeding the audience information and building tension. The main action alternates between a field (where Leah talks to Phil) and a wood (where the group gathers)."
findings.issue: The description is broadly accurate but slightly misleading about Act 4's structure. Acts 1-3 each have four scenes (Street, Field, Wood, Field); Act 4 has only two scenes (Street, Field with Richard) — there is no wood scene and no second field scene in Act 4. The lesson's description implies each act follows the same pattern, which is not quite true for Act 4. This is a minor structural inaccuracy rather than a serious error, but students asked about Act 4's structure could be misled.
findings.correction: Acts 1-3 each cycle through: Street (Mark and Jan), Field (Leah and Phil), Wood (whole group), Field (Leah and Phil). Act 4 breaks this pattern with only two scenes: Street (Mark and Jan) and Field (Richard and Phil — Leah has disappeared). The wood scene is absent in Act 4, reflecting the group's dissolution.
findings.source: RevisionWorld Structure and Setting page ('Act 4 breaks the pattern with only 2 scenes: Scene 1: Street; Scene 2: Field (Phil and Richard)').

findings.claim: "Cathy, who volunteers to threaten a postman and later tortures Adam with a cigarette, is the most extreme example of obedient cruelty."
findings.issue: Same error as DNA-002 in different form. The cigarette torture is from Act 1's initial bullying of Adam (before Cathy's specific Act 3 role); it is not a distinct Act 3 event Cathy performs. Cathy's extreme violence in Act 3 is overseeing Brian's suffocation of Adam with a plastic bag, not cigarette torture. Additionally, Cathy does not 'threaten a postman' — she tricks a postman into handling Adam's jumper at the sorting office to get his DNA on it. Threatening the postman is not confirmed by sources; the characterisation of her action as 'threat' misrepresents the method.
findings.correction: Cathy's extreme cruelty examples should be: (1) taking initiative to frame the postman by getting him to handle Adam's jumper (Act 2 period); (2) overseeing Brian's killing of Adam with a plastic bag in Act 3; (3) becoming the school's violent dominant bully by Act 4 (rumoured to have cut off a first-year's finger). The cigarette torture belongs to Act 1's collective bullying, not a specific Cathy-authored Act 3 act.
findings.source: GradeSaver summary; LitCharts summary; RevisionWorld characters.

findings.location: Section: Phil — recurring food motif description
findings.claim: "an ice cream in Act 1, a muffin in Act 2, chips in Act 3. These recurring motifs of consumption make Phil appear absurdly calm while chaos surrounds him."
findings.issue: The assigned food per act is likely reversed or incorrectly sequenced. Multiple sources (LitCharts scene summaries, GCSE study blogs, RevisionWorld) indicate Phil has a muffin in Act 1 Scene 1 (wood), ice cream in Act 1 Scene 2 (field), chips and/or toffo in later scenes. One widely cited description places the ice cream specifically in Act 1's field scene, the muffin in Act 1's wood/opening. 'Ice cream in Act 1, muffin in Act 2, chips in Act 3' does not align with the Act 1 pattern where both a muffin and ice cream appear in different scenes within Act 1. This could mislead a student who memorises 'Phil eats a muffin in Act 2' when muffin references appear in Act 1.
findings.correction: Phil's food motif spans individual scenes within acts, not one food type per act. In Act 1 he eats a muffin (Scene 1/wood) and ice cream (Scene 2/field). In later acts he eats chips, toffo, and other snacks. By Act 4, he eats nothing — signalling Leah's departure has broken him. The lesson should avoid assigning single food types to whole acts.
findings.source: LitCharts scene summaries; GCSE study blog (jpgayfordefm.wordpress.com); StageAgent; RevisionWorld characters page confirming Phil 'eats ice-cream, Starburst, waffles' across the play.

findings.location: Section: The Four-Act Structure — opening description
findings.claim: "Each act is preceded by a short prologue scene between Mark and Jan on a street." (Implying all four acts follow the same full cycle through all three locations.)
findings.issue: The claim that each act is preceded by a Mark-and-Jan street scene is accurate. However, the broader description of the structure implies all four acts complete the same full cycle (Street → Field → Wood → Field), which is not true for Act 4. Act 4 has only two scenes (Street, then Field with Richard) — no wood scene, no second field scene. While the lesson doesn't explicitly state Act 4 has four scenes, the description could mislead students into thinking the pattern is identical across all four acts.
findings.correction: Acts 1-3 each have four scenes (Street, Field, Wood, Field). Act 4 deviates — only two scenes (Street, then Field with Richard replacing Leah). The structural contraction in Act 4 is itself significant: the wood has disappeared along with the group, and the field now contains Richard rather than Leah.
findings.source: RevisionWorld Structure and Setting page confirms Act 4 has two scenes only; confirmed by GradeSaver and multiple study sources.

findings.location: Section: The Four-Act Structure — description of acts getting shorter
findings.claim: "The four acts are not equal in length. Acts 1 and 2 are the longest, establishing the crime and the cover-up. Act 3 is shorter but more intense, delivering the reversal of Adam's survival. Act 4 is the shortest — a compressed, devastating coda that shows the aftermath."
findings.issue: The length comparison is broadly accurate in dramatic terms. However, the structural description implies acts have equal numbers of scenes but differ in content length, when in fact Act 4 structurally has only two scenes (Street and Field) versus four scenes in Acts 1-3. The lesson does not make this explicit, which is a minor omission rather than an error per se. For a lesson specifically about structure, it is a noticeable gap that Act 4's structural deviation (only 2 scenes, no wood scene) is not mentioned.
findings.correction: Add that Act 4 has only two scenes (Street and Field) rather than four, making it structurally as well as thematically compressed. The absence of the wood scene in Act 4 is a key structural choice: the group has dissolved, so there is no group gathering location to return to.

findings.location: Section: Quotation Strategies — short quotations list
findings.claim: Examples include: "Phil's 'silence,' Leah's 'bonobos,' John Tate banning the word 'dead,' Cathy going into 'television.'"
findings.issue: Same error as DNA-004/DNA-005. 'Cathy going into television' is taught here as a memorisable short quotation, embedding the factual error (that Cathy's Act 4 fate is a TV career) directly into exam technique advice. Students who follow this guidance will cite an inaccurate plot fact in their exams. Cathy's Act 4 fate is violent school dominance and rumoured sadistic violence, not a media career.
findings.correction: Replace 'Cathy going into television' with an accurate reference to her Act 4 fate: e.g., 'Cathy's rumoured violence against first-years' or 'Cathy taking charge' or 'Cathy's finger' (the rumoured cutting-off of a first-year's finger, which is the confirmed Act 4 Cathy reference from the play). If 'television' is used, it should be qualified as a reference to her Act 2 TV interview appearance, not an Act 4 career.
findings.source: GradeSaver; RevisionWorld; StageAgent — all confirm Cathy's end-of-play position is violent school dominance.

findings.location: Section: What Happened to the Others
findings.claim: "Danny and Lou have faded into the background, their passivity now permanent."
findings.issue: For Danny, this is incomplete. Multiple sources confirm that in Act 4, Richard specifically tells Phil that Danny is doing work experience at a dentist's but hates it because open mouths remind him of holes one could fall into — a direct psychological consequence of the grille incident. This is a notable, confirmed Act 4 detail that the lesson omits, leaving students without a specific Danny reference for the exam. It is not a factual error but a significant omission from a lesson covering Act 4 outcomes.
findings.correction: Add: Richard reports in Act 4 that Danny is doing a work experience placement at a dentist's but hates it because the open mouths remind him of holes — a psychologically resonant echo of Adam's fall through the grille. This is confirmed by GradeSaver and multiple study sources as one of Richard's specific Act 4 reports to Phil.
findings.source: GradeSaver character list; GradeSaver Act 3 pages 49-61 summary; RevisionWorld characters page.

most_critical: DNA-001 (HIGH, OCR Acts 1-2): Adam's socks burned, not his shirt — and 'plastic bag over his head' is not part of Act 1 bullying, it is Phil's Act 3 killing method. Two errors in one sentence.

DNA-002 (HIGH, OCR Act 3): Cathy's cigarette torture scene in Act 3 does not exist — cigarettes were stubbed on Adam in the original Act 1 bullying. Act 3 violence is Phil demonstrating plastic bag suffocation, then sending Cathy/Brian to kill Adam off-stage.

DNA-003 (MEDIUM, AQA Acts 1-2): Phil's cover-up plan wrongly stated as including 'a man living rough as a fake witness' — the plan involves a false postman report by Brian; 'man living rough' confuses the plan with Adam (found in Act 3 living rough in a hedge).

DNA-004/005/011 (MEDIUM, AQA Acts 3-4 + Character Analysis + Exam Technique): Cathy's Act 4 fate described as 'moved into television' / 'going into television' — she becomes a violent school bully, not a TV professional. This error appears three times in AQA lessons and is embedded in exam quotation advice.

boards_most_affected.AQA: 4 medium/high findings — primarily the Cathy television-career error (appears 3 times in different lessons) and the Phil plan mis-description
boards_most_affected.OCR: 5 findings — the socks/shirt error and the invented Act 3 cigarette scene are high-severity; the repeated cigarette misattribution also appears in the Context lesson
